set1.q: A 63-year-old woman with chest pain after a car accident that killed her sister has ST elevation and an elevated troponin; stress cardiomyopathy is suspected. Her pain has eased and she is hemodynamically stable in the emergency department. Which disposition is most appropriate?
opts: Admit to cardiology

Correct. Even though her pain has eased and she is stable, Takotsubo mimics acute coronary syndrome with no initial reliable differences, so she is evaluated and treated on established acute coronary syndrome protocols and admitted to cardiology. Treatment is then empiric and supportive, and most patients completely recover.
Discharge home today

Feeling better does not make discharge safe: with ST elevation and an elevated troponin, she cannot yet be told apart from acute coronary syndrome, so she is admitted to cardiology. Tell: the diagnosis is confirmed only by catheterization, which has not happened yet.
Outpatient follow-up only

Outpatient follow-up skips the acute coronary syndrome evaluation she needs; the syndrome mimics acute coronary syndrome, so its protocols apply and she is admitted to cardiology. Tell: elevated troponin plus ST elevation means admission, whatever the suspected cause.
Refer for transplant listing

Transplant listing has no place in Takotsubo, where treatment is empiric and supportive and most patients completely recover. She is admitted to cardiology under acute coronary syndrome protocols. Tell: an expected full recovery rules out transplant.

set1.q: A 63-year-old woman with dilated cardiomyopathy comes to clinic with mild breathlessness on exertion. Her examination shows trace ankle edema and clear lungs. Her B-type natriuretic peptide is 60 pg/mL. What does this natriuretic peptide result indicate?
opts: Myocarditis is confirmed

A natriuretic peptide cannot confirm myocarditis; inflammatory processes are identified with gadolinium-enhanced cardiac magnetic resonance imaging. Her level of 60 pg/mL is below 100, which excludes heart failure. Tell: this test speaks to filling pressure, not to the cause.
Filling pressure is raised

Raised filling pressure releases B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) and pushes the level up; an elevated level indicates increased left ventricular filling pressure and dysfunction. Her 60 pg/mL is low. Tell: a level below 100 pg/mL excludes heart failure, so raised pressure is not shown.
Heart failure is unlikely

Correct. B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) is released when ventricular filling pressures are high, and a level below 100 pg/mL excludes heart failure. Her value of 60 pg/mL, with clear lungs and only trace edema, makes heart failure an unlikely cause of her mild exertional breathlessness.
Heart failure is confirmed

An elevated B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) indicates raised left ventricular filling pressure and dysfunction, but her level of 60 pg/mL is below the 100 pg/mL threshold that excludes heart failure. Tell: the number points away from heart failure, not toward it.

set1.q: A 54-year-old man has stable dilated cardiomyopathy of two years' duration with no systemic illness and no recent change in his heart function. He has read about heart biopsies online and asks whether he should have one. What is the role of a heart muscle biopsy for him?
opts: Not routine and rarely useful

Correct. Endocardial biopsy is not used routinely in dilated cardiomyopathy and is rarely useful. Its indications are recent onset of rapidly deteriorating cardiac function or a history of systemic disease that can involve the heart, and this man has stable disease with neither.
Required to confirm every case

Biopsy is not required to confirm dilated cardiomyopathy; it is not used routinely and is rarely useful. Gadolinium-enhanced cardiac magnetic resonance imaging is the test that helps identify inflammatory, ischemic or infiltrative processes. Tell: with stable disease for two years, there is nothing for a biopsy to answer.
The gold standard for his disease

Biopsy is not the gold standard for dilated cardiomyopathy; it is described as rarely useful and is not used routinely. Its indications are rapid deterioration or systemic disease such as hemochromatosis, sarcoidosis or amyloidosis. Tell: a test that is rarely useful cannot be the gold standard for the disease.
The first test before echocardiography

Biopsy is not a first-line test in dilated cardiomyopathy; it is not used routinely and is kept for recent rapid deterioration or systemic disease with possible cardiac involvement. Tell: his stable course and lack of systemic illness meet neither indication.

set1.q: A 25-year-old woman has newly diagnosed hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with a septum of 2.2 cm and occasional palpitations. Her cardiologist wants to judge her risk of ventricular arrhythmia and sudden cardiac death. Which test assesses that risk?
opts: A repeat chest radiograph

A chest radiograph does not record rhythm and cannot grade arrhythmia risk. Ambulatory electrocardiogram monitoring for 24 to 48 hours assesses the risk of ventricular arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death. Tell: arrhythmia risk is measured by recording the rhythm.
Ambulatory rhythm monitoring

Correct. Ambulatory electrocardiogram monitoring for 24 to 48 hours should be performed in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy to assess the risk of ventricular arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death, the question her cardiologist is asking. Antiarrhythmics such as amiodarone are then used for sudden death prevention.
Cardiac catheterization

Catheterization is not required for diagnosis and is obtained when invasive therapy, a pacemaker or surgery, is planned. Arrhythmia and sudden death risk are assessed with 24 to 48 hours of ambulatory electrocardiogram monitoring. Tell: no procedure is planned, so catheterization has no role.
A genetic testing panel

Genetic testing is available in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy but does not influence treatment, and it is not the test for arrhythmia risk. Ambulatory electrocardiogram monitoring for 24 to 48 hours assesses that risk. Tell: to judge ventricular arrhythmia risk, record the rhythm.

set1.q: A 67-year-old woman is recovering in hospital from stress cardiomyopathy that followed news of her son's serious illness. Her chest pain has resolved, and she asks whether her heart will stay damaged. Which answer about her prognosis is most accurate?
opts: Poorest outlook of any type

The poorest outlook is the opposite of the Takotsubo course: most patients completely recover. Tell: her resolved chest pain and supportive treatment fit a syndrome with an expected full recovery, which answers her worry about lasting damage.
Most patients recover completely

Correct. Most patients with Takotsubo cardiomyopathy completely recover. Care in hospital is empiric and supportive, with beta blockers, anticoagulation if a left ventricular thrombus is present and diuretics if heart failure is present, so she can be told her heart is expected to recover.
Half die within five years

Half dying within five years is not the Takotsubo outlook; most patients completely recover after empiric, supportive treatment. Tell: Takotsubo is the cardiomyopathy with the good prognosis, which is the answer to her question.
It always progresses to failure

Takotsubo does not routinely progress to heart failure; diuretics are used only if heart failure is present, and most patients completely recover. Tell: always is the giveaway, since the expected course is recovery.

set1.q: A 27-year-old man admitted with presumed viral myocarditis keeps deteriorating despite full medical treatment. Coronary angiography is normal, and valvular, toxic and ischemic causes of heart failure have been excluded. Which test establishes the diagnosis?
opts: Serum troponin

Serum troponin indicates cardiac myonecrosis but does not identify its cause, so it cannot establish myocarditis. Endomyocardial biopsy is the gold standard. Tell: his deterioration despite treatment, with other causes excluded, is the textbook indication for biopsy.
Endomyocardial biopsy

Correct. Endomyocardial biopsy is the gold standard and is used to establish the diagnosis once other causes of heart failure are excluded, as his have been. It is recommended in acute deterioration of heart function of unknown origin that is not responding to medical treatment, which describes his course.
Cardiac catheterization

Cardiac angiography rules out coronary ischemia as a cause of new-onset heart failure, and his was already normal. Endomyocardial biopsy is what establishes myocarditis. Tell: repeating the exclusion step adds nothing; the next step is tissue.
Chest radiograph

The chest X-ray in myocarditis is nonspecific and may only show cardiomegaly. Endomyocardial biopsy is the gold standard that establishes the diagnosis. Tell: a nonspecific film cannot establish a specific diagnosis.

set1.q: A 58-year-old woman received mediastinal radiation and chemotherapy for a chest cancer 15 years ago. She now has progressive exercise intolerance, orthopnea (breathlessness lying flat), ascites and swollen legs. Echocardiogram shows stiff ventricles of normal size, marked atrial enlargement and abnormal diastolic function with a preserved ejection fraction. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Dilated cardiomyopathy

Dilated cardiomyopathy would show dilated ventricles, but hers are normal in size with a preserved ejection fraction. Her stiff ventricles, marked atrial enlargement and abnormal diastolic function after mediastinal radiation and chemotherapy fit restrictive cardiomyopathy. Tell: normal-sized ventricles plus big atria means restrictive.
Acute myocarditis

Acute myocarditis does not fit a slow course years after cancer treatment. Mediastinal radiation and chemotherapy are named causes of restrictive cardiomyopathy, which often presents at an advanced stage with pronounced cardiopulmonary symptoms. Tell: a remote treatment history plus stiff ventricles points to restriction.
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy

Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is not linked to radiation or chemotherapy, and her picture is stiff ventricles of normal size with big atria. Treatment-related cardiotoxicity, through inflammation and fibrosis, causes restrictive cardiomyopathy. Tell: prior mediastinal radiation and chemotherapy is the named restrictive clue.
Restrictive cardiomyopathy

Correct. Mediastinal radiation and chemotherapy are treatment-related causes of restrictive cardiomyopathy, with chemotherapy leading to inflammation, then fibrosis and restriction. These patients may have a prior history of radiation or chemotherapy and often present at an advanced stage, as she does with stiff ventricles and big atria.

set1.q: A 29-year-old man with acute myocarditis after a viral illness has fluid retention with bilateral leg edema and crackles, but his blood pressure is stable. He is receiving supportive care. Which medication may be added as needed for his fluid retention?
opts: A thrombolytic drug

A thrombolytic is not on the myocarditis medication list, and nothing in his case involves a clot. The as-needed medications are vasodilators, angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, diuretics, antiarrhythmics and anticoagulation. Tell: fluid retention points to the diuretic.
Alcohol septal ablation

Alcohol septal ablation is a procedure, not a medication, and it is not part of myocarditis care. Fluid retention in myocarditis is managed with a diuretic as part of supportive care. Tell: the question asks for a drug for fluid, which is a diuretic.
A diuretic

Correct. Supportive care is the mainstay of myocarditis treatment, and medications are added as needed for the clinical scenario. For his fluid retention, with leg edema and crackles, that means a diuretic; vasodilators, angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, antiarrhythmics and anticoagulation are the other as-needed options.
A positive inotrope

A positive inotrope is not on the myocarditis medication list, and with a stable blood pressure he needs no hemodynamic rescue. The as-needed medication for fluid retention is a diuretic. Tell: match the drug to the problem, and fluid means diuretic.

set1.q: A 23-year-old previously healthy man has breathlessness, chest pain and exercise intolerance ten days after a flulike illness with fever, myalgia and diarrhea. He is tachycardic with a third heart sound (an early diastolic sound just after the second heart sound) and crackles at both bases. Troponin is elevated and coronary angiography is normal. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Acute viral myocarditis

Correct. A previously healthy young man with heart failure symptoms ten days after fever, myalgia and diarrhea fits viral myocarditis, which follows a recent (1 to 2 week) flulike syndrome; young males are particularly susceptible. His tachycardia, third heart sound and crackles match the examination.
Takotsubo cardiomyopathy

Takotsubo is not suggested by this history; his trigger is a flulike illness with fever, myalgia and diarrhea 10 days earlier, the prodrome of viral myocarditis. Tell: a young male with a viral prodrome, low cardiac risk and acute heart failure points to myocarditis.
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy

Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy does not explain acute heart failure arriving 10 days after a flulike illness in a previously healthy man. Viral myocarditis presents exactly this way, with acute decompensation and no underlying cardiac dysfunction. Tell: the timing after a viral illness is the key clue.
Restrictive cardiomyopathy

Restrictive cardiomyopathy does not fit acute heart failure in a previously healthy 23-year-old after a flulike illness. Viral myocarditis follows a 1 to 2 week flulike syndrome with fever, myalgia or gastroenteritis. Tell: his diarrhea counts as gastroenteritis, part of the viral prodrome.

set1.q: A 35-year-old woman with obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy developed severe asthma symptoms when a beta blocker was started, and it was stopped. She still has exertional breathlessness from outflow obstruction. Which medication is the appropriate alternative?
opts: Nifedipine, a vasodilator

Nifedipine is not one of the calcium channel blockers named for outflow tract obstruction; only the nondihydropyridine agents verapamil and diltiazem are, and drugs that reduce afterload may aggravate obstruction. Tell: in this disease the calcium channel blocker must slow the heart and reduce contractility.
Nitroglycerin paste

Nitrates reduce preload or afterload and may increase symptoms by aggravating outflow tract obstruction, so they are avoided if possible. The alternative to a beta blocker is verapamil or diltiazem. Tell: in obstruction, anything that unloads the heart is avoided.
Norepinephrine infusion

Norepinephrine is a positive inotrope, avoided because increased contractility raises the risk of myocardial ischemia and may induce arrhythmias. Verapamil or diltiazem, which reduce contractility, is the alternative. Tell: she needs a negative inotrope, not a positive one.
Verapamil or diltiazem

Correct. With the beta blocker stopped because of her asthma, the other listed medication for outflow tract obstruction is a nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocker, verapamil or diltiazem. Like a beta blocker, it is a negative chronotrope and negative inotrope.

set1.q: A 46-year-old woman with obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy has recurrent palpitations from atrial fibrillation and atrial flutter. She already takes anticoagulation to prevent embolic stroke. Which medication is used to convert her rhythm to sinus and suppress recurrence?
opts: Nitroglycerin

Nitrates reduce preload or afterload and are avoided if possible because they aggravate outflow tract obstruction, and they do not convert a rhythm. Amiodarone converts atrial fibrillation and flutter to sinus rhythm. Tell: rhythm conversion needs an antiarrhythmic.
Epinephrine

Epinephrine is a positive inotrope, avoided because increased contractility raises the risk of myocardial ischemia and may induce arrhythmias. Amiodarone converts atrial fibrillation and flutter and suppresses recurrence. Tell: a drug that may induce arrhythmias cannot be the one that suppresses them.
Amiodarone

Correct. Amiodarone is very effective at converting atrial fibrillation and flutter to sinus rhythm and suppressing recurrence, and it reduces the incidence and risk of sudden cardiac death with or without outflow obstruction. Her anticoagulation already covers stroke prevention; radiofrequency ablation is another option.
Digoxin

Digoxin is a positive inotrope, on the avoid list in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy because it increases contractility and may induce arrhythmias. Amiodarone is the antiarrhythmic that converts and suppresses atrial fibrillation and flutter. Tell: in this disease digoxin is avoided, while amiodarone is used.

set1.q: A 68-year-old woman has crushing chest pain and breathlessness the day after her husband's funeral. She has no hypertension, diabetes or smoking history. The electrocardiogram shows ST elevation with T-wave inversion, troponin is elevated, and echocardiogram shows hypokinesis of the mid and apical segments of the left ventricle. Catheterization shows normal coronary arteries. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Dilated cardiomyopathy

Dilated cardiomyopathy does not fit a sudden presentation the day after a funeral with regional mid and apical hypokinesis. Transient regional left ventricular dysfunction after an emotional stressor, with normal coronaries, is Takotsubo. Tell: a stressor, a regional wall-motion defect and clean coronaries make Takotsubo.
Takotsubo cardiomyopathy

Correct. A postmenopausal woman with chest pain the day after her husband's funeral, no cardiac risk factors, mid and apical hypokinesis and normal coronary arteries has Takotsubo (stress) cardiomyopathy: transient regional systolic dysfunction that mimics acute coronary syndrome without angiographic coronary disease.
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy

Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy does not explain chest pain triggered by grief with regional hypokinesis and normal coronaries. Takotsubo is triggered by a significant emotional or physical stressor, and 90% of cases are postmenopausal women. Tell: death of a loved one is a listed trigger for Takotsubo.
Restrictive cardiomyopathy

Restrictive cardiomyopathy does not present as sudden chest pain after a bereavement. Takotsubo mimics acute coronary syndrome after a stressor, in patients with low or no cardiac risk factors, as in this woman. Tell: no hypertension, diabetes or smoking plus a recent loss points to Takotsubo.

set1.q: A 72-year-old man has months of progressive breathlessness, abdominal swelling and bilateral pedal edema. He prefers to sit upright. Jugular venous pressure is raised and he has a Kussmaul sign (jugular venous pressure rises with inspiration), hepatomegaly and ascites. His electrocardiogram shows low voltage (small complexes) in all leads, and echocardiogram shows normal-sized ventricles, marked biatrial enlargement and a preserved ejection fraction. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy

Takotsubo does not fit months of progressive congestion. His normal-sized ventricles, biatrial enlargement and preserved ejection fraction show impaired diastolic filling with preserved chamber size, the restrictive pattern. Tell: a slowly building right-sided picture with big atria is restrictive.
Restrictive cardiomyopathy

Correct. Right-sided congestion with normal-sized ventricles, marked biatrial enlargement and a preserved ejection fraction is restrictive cardiomyopathy: impaired diastolic filling with preserved chamber size, both atria enlarged and right heart failure often more prominent. Amyloidosis is the most common cause in the United States.
Dilated cardiomyopathy

Dilated cardiomyopathy would show enlarged ventricles, but his are normal in size with a preserved ejection fraction. Restrictive cardiomyopathy keeps chamber size and systolic function reasonably preserved while both atria enlarge. Tell: big atria with normal-sized ventricles is restrictive.
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy

Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is not suggested: his ventricles are normal in size and the dominant picture is right-sided congestion with biatrial enlargement. In restrictive cardiomyopathy wall thickness is normal or only slightly increased, and right heart failure is often more prominent. Tell: right-sided failure plus big atria points to restriction.

set1.q: A 64-year-old woman with dilated cardiomyopathy has breathlessness on exertion and peripheral edema. On examination her neck veins distend when firm pressure is held over her right upper abdomen, a sign called hepatojugular reflux (neck-vein distension with firm pressure over the liver). Which additional finding is expected with this degree of congestion?
opts: Congestive enlargement of the liver

Correct. Alongside hepatojugular reflux, the gastrointestinal findings of dilated cardiomyopathy include congestive hepatomegaly and ascites. They reflect venous congestion, which also gives jugular vein distention, an enlarged liver and spleen, and dependent pitting edema like hers.
A small, soft, nonpalpable liver

A small liver is the opposite of what congestion does: in dilated cardiomyopathy the gastrointestinal findings are congestive hepatomegaly, hepatojugular reflux and ascites, with the liver and spleen enlarged from venous congestion. Tell: hepatojugular reflux and an enlarged liver travel together.
A pulsatile mass in the epigastrium

A pulsatile epigastric mass is not among the congestive findings. With hepatojugular reflux, the expected gastrointestinal findings of dilated cardiomyopathy are congestive hepatomegaly and ascites. Tell: venous congestion enlarges the liver and fills the abdomen with fluid; it does not create a pulsating mass.
Flank bruising from bleeding

Flank bruising has nothing to do with venous congestion. Dilated cardiomyopathy with hepatojugular reflux is expected to show congestive hepatomegaly and ascites, along with dependent pitting edema. Tell: congestion causes swelling and enlargement, not bruising.

set1.q: A 69-year-old woman with right-sided heart failure, ascites and a raised jugular venous pressure has cardiac magnetic resonance imaging to decide between restrictive cardiomyopathy and constrictive pericarditis. Which imaging finding would point to constrictive pericarditis instead?
opts: Marked atrial enlargement

Marked enlargement of one or both atria is a feature of restrictive cardiomyopathy on echo, so it does not point to pericarditis. The finding on cardiac magnetic resonance imaging that does is pericardial thickening. Tell: look for a pericardial finding to diagnose a pericardial disease.
Preserved ejection fraction

A preserved left ventricular ejection fraction is typical of restrictive cardiomyopathy, which keeps it until late stages, so it does not separate the two. Pericardial thickening on magnetic resonance imaging points to constrictive pericarditis. Tell: shared features cannot decide between them.
Normal ventricular cavity size

Normal or near normal left ventricular cavity size is expected in restrictive cardiomyopathy and does not favor pericarditis. The magnetic resonance imaging finding for constrictive pericarditis is pericardial thickening. Tell: the deciding image is of the pericardium, not the ventricle.
Pericardial thickening

Correct. Echocardiography alone cannot separate restrictive cardiomyopathy from constrictive pericarditis, so cardiac magnetic resonance imaging is used, and pericardial thickening points to pericarditis. Big atria, a preserved ejection fraction and normal cavity size are restrictive features that do not decide the question.

set1.q: A 41-year-old man with obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy comes to the emergency department with exertional chest pressure. His electrocardiogram shows left ventricular hypertrophy without acute changes, and a clinician reaches for a chest pain order set. Which medication should be avoided?
opts: Nitroglycerin

Correct. In obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, drugs that reduce preload or afterload, such as nitrates, may increase symptoms by aggravating outflow tract obstruction, so nitroglycerin from a chest pain order set should be avoided if possible. A beta blocker such as metoprolol is the initial medication for his obstruction instead.
Metoprolol

Metoprolol, a beta blocker, is the initial medication for outflow tract obstruction; it reduces heart rate and enhances diastolic filling. It is used, not avoided. Tell: the danger in a chest pain order set for this disease is the nitrate.
Verapamil

Verapamil, a nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocker, treats outflow tract obstruction as a negative chronotrope and inotrope. The drug to avoid is the nitrate, which reduces preload and afterload. Tell: drugs that slow and soften the heart help; drugs that unload it hurt.
Amiodarone

Amiodarone is used in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy to reduce the incidence and risk of sudden cardiac death and to convert atrial fibrillation and flutter. It is not the drug to avoid; nitroglycerin is. Tell: the avoided drugs are nitrates and positive inotropes.

set1.q: A 75-year-old man is newly diagnosed with restrictive cardiomyopathy caused by hemochromatosis, with iron deposited in the heart tissue. He has congestion and fatigue. Which is the first principle of his management?
opts: An inotrope to raise output

An inotrope is not on the restrictive cardiomyopathy list; the drugs used are cautious diuretics, beta blockers or cardioselective calcium channel blockers, and anticoagulants. The first principle is treating the underlying disorder. Tell: the listed drugs slow and relax the heart rather than push it harder.
A high-intensity exercise program

A high-intensity exercise program does not treat hemochromatosis or the stiff ventricle. Management starts by treating the underlying disorder. Tell: he has a known cause, iron deposited in heart tissue, and the first principle is to treat it.
Treat the underlying disorder

Correct. Management of restrictive cardiomyopathy begins with treating the underlying disorder, here hemochromatosis. Diuretics are then used with caution for his congestion, beta blockers or verapamil and diltiazem may improve filling, and anticoagulants or a pacemaker are added as needed.
Septal myectomy for relief

Septal myectomy is not part of restrictive cardiomyopathy care; the steps are treating the underlying disorder, cautious diuretics, rate-slowing drugs, anticoagulants, a pacemaker and transplantation. Tell: his problem is iron in the heart muscle, so the cause is treated, not cut away.

set1.q: An 86-year-old woman with end-stage cardiomyopathy has breathlessness at rest, edema and fatigue despite maximal tolerated therapy. She is not a transplant or device candidate and says she wants comfort at home. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Stop all of her symptom medicines

Palliative care actively manages dyspnea, fatigue and edema; it does not withdraw symptom relief. The next step is a goals-of-care discussion and hospice referral. Tell: comfort care still treats symptoms, especially in a frail elderly patient.
Add an assist device urgently

She is not a device candidate, and her goal is comfort at home. Elderly care focuses on symptom control and quality of life, with palliative care discussions in advanced stages and hospice referral in end-stage disease. Tell: her stated wish and end-stage disease point to palliative care.
Discuss goals of care and hospice

Correct. She has end-stage cardiomyopathy, is not a transplant or device candidate and wants comfort at home. Palliative care covers symptom management of dyspnea, fatigue and edema, advance care planning and goals-of-care discussions, caregiver support and hospice referral in end-stage disease.
Refer for heart transplant listing

She is not a transplant candidate and has asked for comfort at home. In end-stage cardiomyopathy the step is advance care planning, goals-of-care discussion and hospice referral. Tell: when advanced therapies are off the table, palliative care leads.

set1.q: A 33-year-old man with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy confirmed by echocardiography has typical findings and no plans for surgery or a device. A colleague suggests cardiac catheterization to complete the work-up. When is cardiac catheterization indicated in this condition?
opts: Always, to rule out coronary disease

Catheterization is not routine in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy; it is obtained only when a pacemaker or surgery is planned. Exercise echocardiography can assess exercise-induced ischemia without it. Tell: always is the wrong word for a test reserved for planned procedures.
Only if the murmur is very loud

Murmur loudness is not an indication for catheterization. It is obtained only when invasive therapy, a pacemaker or surgery, is planned. Tell: the trigger is a planned procedure, not an examination finding, and he has no procedure planned.
Only if surgery or a pacemaker is planned

Correct. Cardiac catheterization is not required for diagnosis of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy; it is obtained when invasive modalities of therapy, a pacemaker or surgery, are planned. With his diagnosis already confirmed and no such plans, it adds nothing now.
Always, to confirm the diagnosis

Catheterization is not required for diagnosis; his was already confirmed by echocardiography, and cardiac magnetic resonance imaging helps when echo is questionable. Tell: catheterization waits for a plan for a pacemaker or surgery.

set1.q: A 22-year-old man has breathlessness on exertion and occasional palpitations. His father has hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. His pulse shows pulsus bisferiens (a double systolic peak), the apical impulse is forceful and sustained, and a fourth heart sound (a late diastolic sound just before the first heart sound) is present. Which is the typical diagnostic test of choice?
opts: Chest radiograph

The chest X-ray may be normal in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, so it cannot confirm the diagnosis. Echocardiography is the typical diagnostic test of choice, measuring the wall thickness that defines the disease. Tell: a test that may be normal cannot be the test of choice.
Echocardiography

Correct. Echocardiography is the typical diagnostic test of choice for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, confirming it when unexplained left ventricular wall thickness is 1.5 cm or more. It also shows asymmetric septal hypertrophy, a small cavity, systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve and left atrial enlargement.
Cardiac catheterization

Cardiac catheterization is invasive and is not the test of choice. Echocardiography confirms hypertrophic cardiomyopathy by showing unexplained left ventricular wall thickness of 1.5 cm or more. Tell: his findings call for imaging the wall, which echo does noninvasively.
Genetic testing

Genetic testing is not the diagnostic test of choice. The diagnosis is confirmed by echocardiography showing unexplained left ventricular wall thickness of 1.5 cm or more, usually asymmetric and septal. Tell: the diagnosis is made by measuring the heart, even with a family history like his.

set1.q: A 55-year-old man has progressive breathlessness on exertion, fatigue and swelling of both legs. The apical impulse is displaced laterally, a third heart sound (an early diastolic sound just after the second heart sound) is present, and there is a soft murmur at the apex. Which echocardiogram finding would support dilated cardiomyopathy?
opts: Midsegment and apical hypokinesis alone

Hypokinesis confined to the mid and apical segments is a limited regional pattern; dilated cardiomyopathy shows dilated, thin walls with an ejection fraction below 40% and hypokinetic chambers. Segmental wall-motion abnormalities can occur, but dilation is the prominent feature. Tell: look for dilation, not a regional defect alone.
Dilated thin walls with a reduced ejection fraction

Correct. His displaced apical impulse, third heart sound and apical murmur fit dilated cardiomyopathy, and the supporting echocardiogram shows dilated, thin walls (the prominent feature) with an ejection fraction below 40%. Hypokinetic chambers, dilation of up to all four chambers, mitral or tricuspid regurgitation and sometimes thrombus may also appear.
A thick septum and a small left ventricular cavity

A thick septum with a small cavity is the opposite of the dilated picture. Dilated cardiomyopathy shows dilated, thin walls, an ejection fraction below 40% and hypokinetic chambers. Tell: dilated means big chambers with thin walls, not a small, thick-walled one.
Normal cavity size with large atria and stiff walls

Normal cavity size with large atria does not support dilated cardiomyopathy, whose echo shows dilated, thin walls, possibly all four chambers dilated and an ejection fraction below 40%. Tell: in dilated disease the ventricles themselves are enlarged and weak.

set1.q: A 50-year-old man is newly diagnosed with dilated cardiomyopathy after a viral illness. He is in sinus rhythm, blood pressure is 118/72, and his ejection fraction is 30%. No thrombus is seen on echocardiogram. Which pair of drug classes belongs to his guideline-directed medical therapy?
opts: Anticoagulant and antiarrhythmic started for everyone

Anticoagulants and antiarrhythmics are on the dilated cardiomyopathy drug list, but they are not part of adult guideline-directed therapy, and he has no thrombus and is in sinus rhythm. The guideline-directed pair is a beta blocker with an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor. Tell: for everyone does not fit drugs given for a specific need.
Verapamil and a nitrate to relax the thick ventricle

Verapamil is used for outflow obstruction in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and may help filling in restrictive disease; his ventricle is dilated with an ejection fraction of 30%, not thick. The guideline-directed pair is a beta blocker with an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor. Tell: there is no thick ventricle here to relax.
A diuretic alone, until symptoms settle to baseline

Diuretics belong to guideline-directed therapy, but alone they leave out the beta blocker and angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor, and no fluid retention is described in him. Tell: guideline-directed therapy is a combination built on a beta blocker and an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor.
Beta blocker and angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor

Correct. Guideline-directed medical therapy for adults with cardiomyopathy includes angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, beta blockers, angiotensin receptor blockers and diuretics, and both drugs in this pair are on the dilated cardiomyopathy drug list. His stable blood pressure, sinus rhythm and ejection fraction of 30% fit starting them.

set1.q: A 30-year-old man with obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is stable on a beta blocker. He drinks six to eight beers on most weekend nights and asks whether he needs to change anything. Which counseling point is most appropriate?
opts: No limit while on his beta blocker

A beta blocker is the initial medication for outflow tract obstruction, but it does not cancel the advice to avoid excess alcohol. Tell: medication and self-care work together, and the education list still says to avoid excess alcohol.
Restrict his daily fluid intake

Restricting fluids runs against the advice to maintain hydration and avoid dehydration in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. The change he needs is to avoid excess alcohol. Tell: the question is about his drinking, and the advice is to cut alcohol, not water.
Restrict salt; alcohol is fine

Sodium restriction to less than 2 g/day is education for dilated cardiomyopathy, not the key point here, and alcohol is not fine: patients with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy are told to avoid excess alcohol. Tell: his weekend drinking is the problem to address.
Avoid drinking alcohol to excess

Correct. Six to eight beers on most weekend nights is excess, and patient education in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy includes avoiding excess alcohol consumption, alongside maintaining hydration and keeping to mild to moderate, noncompetitive activity. Being stable on a beta blocker does not change that advice.

set1.q: A 66-year-old woman with stress cardiomyopathy confirmed by normal coronary arteries at catheterization is stable, with no ventricular thrombus and no signs of heart failure. Which medication is helpful in her supportive treatment?
opts: An inotrope infusion

An inotrope is not part of Takotsubo supportive care, and she is stable without heart failure. The supportive medication listed as helpful is a beta blocker, with diuretics only if heart failure develops. Tell: a stable patient with no failure and no thrombus gets a beta blocker.
A thrombolytic drug

Catheterization already showed normal coronary arteries, so there is no coronary clot to dissolve, and she has no ventricular thrombus. Beta blockers are the helpful supportive medication. Tell: in Takotsubo the coronaries are clean, so a clot-dissolving drug has no target.
Amyl nitrite by inhalation

Amyl nitrite decreases afterload and is a maneuver that increases the murmur of obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy; it is not a treatment for stress cardiomyopathy. Beta blockers are the helpful supportive medication. Tell: amyl nitrite belongs to the murmur table, not to Takotsubo care.
A beta blocker

Correct. Takotsubo treatment is empiric and supportive and depends on the presentation: beta blockers are helpful, anticoagulation is added only for a left ventricular thrombus, and diuretics only for heart failure. With neither thrombus nor heart failure, a beta blocker is the helpful medication for her, and most patients completely recover.

mis.A thrombolytic drug: competing diagnosis: treated as a coronary occlusion despite normal arteries

set1.q: A 74-year-old man with restrictive cardiomyopathy is found to have cardiac amyloidosis, with amyloid protein deposited in the heart tissue. He has breathlessness, leg edema and ascites. Which electrocardiogram finding is expected with this infiltrative disease?
opts: Left axis deviation

Left axis deviation is not the finding described for amyloid infiltration. The restrictive electrocardiogram may show low QRS voltage in amyloidosis, with atrial fibrillation and bundle branch blocks also common. Tell: infiltrative disease is tied to low voltage.
ST elevation

ST elevation is not part of the restrictive or amyloid electrocardiogram. In amyloidosis infiltrative disease the tracing may show low QRS voltage, often with atrial fibrillation or a bundle branch block. Tell: amyloid means small complexes, not a raised segment.
Low QRS voltage

Correct. The electrocardiogram in restrictive cardiomyopathy depends on the stage and diagnosis, and it may show low QRS voltage in amyloidosis infiltrative disease. Rhythm disorders such as atrial fibrillation and conduction disorders such as bundle branch blocks are also common.
Prominent Q waves

Prominent Q waves are not the amyloid finding. Restrictive cardiomyopathy from amyloidosis may show low QRS voltage on the electrocardiogram, along with rhythm and conduction disorders, while the chest X-ray shows cardiomegaly from atrial enlargement. Tell: an infiltrated heart gives low voltage.

set1.q: A 66-year-old woman with dilated cardiomyopathy develops a new holosystolic murmur heard best at the apex that radiates to the left axilla. Her ventricle has continued to enlarge on serial echocardiograms. Which complication best accounts for the new murmur?
opts: Pericardial thickening from constriction

Pericardial thickening is not a complication of dilated cardiomyopathy. Her new murmur reflects valve regurgitation from a distorted valve apparatus as the ventricle dilates, with mitral regurgitation appearing earlier. Tell: a new murmur in an enlarging ventricle means a distorted, leaking valve.
Functional mitral regurgitation from dilation

Correct. As the ventricle in dilated cardiomyopathy keeps dilating, the valve apparatus is distorted, and mitral regurgitation (which appears earlier) and tricuspid regurgitation commonly develop. Her new holosystolic apical murmur is that mitral regurgitation, and rising end-systolic volumes then drive further dilation.
Outflow obstruction from a thick septum

A thick septum does not fit dilated cardiomyopathy, which increases cardiac mass with little or no wall hypertrophy. Her new murmur is mitral regurgitation from distortion of the valve apparatus. Tell: an enlarging, dilated ventricle stretches the valve rather than obstructing outflow.
Tricuspid regurgitation into the axilla

Tricuspid regurgitation also develops in dilated cardiomyopathy, but mitral regurgitation appears earlier, matching a new murmur heard best at the apex. Tell: the mitral valve is the first to leak as the ventricle dilates, and her murmur is apical.

set1.q: A 70-year-old woman with restrictive cardiomyopathy has pulmonary and systemic congestion, with crackles and leg edema. A diuretic is being started. Which statement about diuretic use in her is most accurate?
opts: Use with caution; stiff ventricles need preload

Correct. Diuretics are used for her pulmonary and systemic congestion, but with caution, because they lower preload and noncompliant ventricles depend on preload to maintain cardiac output. Beta blockers or verapamil and diltiazem may also help by lengthening left ventricular filling time.
Contraindicated in any restrictive disease

Diuretics are not contraindicated; they are the listed treatment for pulmonary and systemic congestion in restrictive cardiomyopathy. They are simply used with caution because noncompliant ventricles depend on preload. Tell: caution is not a contraindication.
Give aggressively to fully dry the lungs

Aggressive diuresis drops the preload that noncompliant ventricles rely on to maintain cardiac output. Diuretics are used for congestion, but cautiously. Tell: in restrictive disease the goal is relief of congestion without stripping the preload the heart needs.
Only useful once the ejection fraction falls

Diuretics are given for pulmonary and systemic congestion, which she has now; the indication is congestion, not a falling ejection fraction. The caution is about lowering preload in noncompliant ventricles. Tell: treat the congestion that is present, carefully.

set1.q: A 65-year-old woman developed chest pain and dyspnea during a hurricane evacuation. She has ST elevation, an elevated troponin and B-type natriuretic peptide, and an echocardiogram showing akinesis of the left ventricular apex. Which test confirms stress cardiomyopathy?
opts: Cardiac catheterization

Correct. Her stressor (a hurricane evacuation), chest pain, ST elevation, raised troponin and B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP), and apical akinesis all fit stress cardiomyopathy but also mimic acute coronary syndrome. The diagnosis is confirmed with cardiac catheterization, which most often shows normal coronary arteries.
Endomyocardial biopsy

Endomyocardial biopsy is not part of the stress cardiomyopathy work-up. Confirmation comes from cardiac catheterization, which most often shows normal coronary arteries. Tell: the question that matters is whether the coronaries are blocked, which only catheterization answers.
Exercise stress test

An exercise stress test does not confirm Takotsubo and is not part of its work-up, which follows acute coronary syndrome protocols. Cardiac catheterization confirms the diagnosis by showing normal coronary arteries. Tell: with ST elevation and raised troponin, the next look is at the coronaries, not a treadmill.
Serial troponin levels

Troponin I and T are usually elevated in Takotsubo, as they are in acute coronary syndrome, so repeating them cannot separate the two. Cardiac catheterization showing normal coronary arteries confirms the diagnosis. Tell: shared markers cannot confirm; the coronary arteries decide.

set1.q: A 64-year-old man with dilated cardiomyopathy takes a beta blocker, an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor and a diuretic. His clinician mentions that digoxin may be added later. Which statement describes the place of digoxin in his treatment?
opts: The first-line drug to start now

Digoxin is not first-line; it is considered a second-line drug in dilated cardiomyopathy, added after core drugs such as his beta blocker and angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor. Tell: the qualifier second-line is attached to digoxin on the drug list.
A drug to avoid in this disease

Digoxin is not avoided in dilated cardiomyopathy; it is on the management list as a second-line drug. Tell: in a dilated, weak ventricle digoxin has a place, but behind the core drugs such as a beta blocker and an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor.
A replacement for his diuretic

Digoxin does not replace a diuretic; diuretics are their own class on the dilated cardiomyopathy drug list, and digoxin is a second-line addition. Tell: second-line drugs are added on, not swapped in for a core drug.
A second-line drug, not first-line

Correct. Digoxin is on the list of drugs used to manage dilated cardiomyopathy but is considered a second-line drug. The rest of the list includes angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, beta-adrenergic blockers, angiotensin receptor blockers, spironolactone, sacubitril/valsartan, nitrates, diuretics, antiarrhythmics and anticoagulants.

set1.q: A 16-year-old girl with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy has had an episode of fainting during basketball practice and brief runs of ventricular tachycardia on monitoring. She wants to keep playing on her competitive school team. Which counseling point is most appropriate?
opts: Activity restriction given her high risk

Correct. Her syncope during basketball identifies a patient at high risk of sudden death, and sudden cardiac death in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy has its highest incidence in preadolescents and adolescents and is related to extreme exertion. Activity restriction for high-risk individuals is the adolescent strategy.
Unrestricted play with extra fluids

Maintaining hydration is advised, but it does not make competitive play safe for a high-risk adolescent. Her exertional syncope and ventricular tachycardia mark high risk of sudden death, so activity restriction applies. Tell: hydration is general advice; restriction is for high-risk patients like her.
Clearance once the murmur softens

The outflow murmur softens with anything that increases blood flow in the heart, such as squatting, so a softer murmur says nothing about her risk. Her syncope identifies high risk of sudden death and calls for activity restriction. Tell: risk is judged by syncope and arrhythmia, not murmur loudness.
Competitive play on a beta blocker

A beta blocker is the initial medication for outflow tract obstruction, but it does not make competitive sport safe for a high-risk adolescent. Sudden death in this disease is related to extreme exertion, so her activity is restricted. Tell: medication treats obstruction; restriction addresses exertional sudden death risk.

set2.q: A 20-year-old man with acute myocarditis after a flulike illness is on the ward with heart failure symptoms. He reports new palpitations, and his nurse notes a brief episode of lightheadedness. Which complication poses the most immediate threat to his life?
opts: Aortic dissection

Aortic dissection is not part of acute myocarditis, and nothing in his story suggests it. His palpitations and lightheadedness fit the arrhythmic risk of myocarditis, ventricular arrhythmias or atrioventricular block, which can cause syncope or sudden cardiac death. Tell: palpitations plus near-fainting means rhythm.
Pericardial thickening

Pericardial thickening is not a complication described for myocarditis and would not explain sudden palpitations with lightheadedness. Those symptoms fit ventricular arrhythmias or atrioventricular block, which can lead to syncope or sudden cardiac death. Tell: the clue is palpitations, a rhythm symptom.
Mitral valve prolapse

Mitral valve prolapse is not part of the myocarditis picture. New palpitations with lightheadedness here signal ventricular arrhythmia or atrioventricular block, which in myocarditis can progress to syncope or sudden cardiac death. Tell: link the symptoms to the arrhythmia, not to a valve.
Ventricular arrhythmia

Correct. In this young man with myocarditis after a flulike illness, new palpitations and a brief episode of lightheadedness point to the arrhythmic danger: palpitations, syncope or sudden cardiac death in myocarditis are due to underlying ventricular arrhythmias or atrioventricular block. Sudden death makes this the most immediate threat.

set2.q: A 24-year-old woman with chest pain and breathlessness after a recent viral illness is being evaluated for myocarditis. Her electrocardiogram shows sinus tachycardia. Which laboratory result would indicate cardiac myonecrosis?
opts: Elevated serum troponin

Correct. In this young woman with chest pain and breathlessness after a viral illness, serum troponin is the indicator of cardiac myonecrosis. Her sinus tachycardia fits the electrocardiogram of myocarditis, and the rest of the work-up looks for leukocytosis and a possibly elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate.
A low white cell count

The blood count in myocarditis shows leukocytosis, a raised white cell count, not a low one, and it does not measure heart muscle injury. Serum troponin indicates cardiac myonecrosis. Tell: leukocytosis is the expected count; troponin is the necrosis marker.
Normal sedimentation rate

The erythrocyte sedimentation rate may be elevated in myocarditis, so a normal value is not the expected finding, and either way it is not the myonecrosis marker. Serum troponin is the indicator of cardiac myonecrosis. Tell: a normal result cannot indicate necrosis.
A low natriuretic peptide

A natriuretic peptide is not the listed myonecrosis marker, and a low value would indicate nothing abnormal. Serum troponin is the indicator of cardiac myonecrosis in the myocarditis work-up. Tell: necrosis raises a marker, and the one named for heart muscle is troponin.

set2.q: A 71-year-old woman admitted with stress cardiomyopathy after a house fire has a repeat echocardiogram that shows a thrombus in the akinetic left ventricular apex. She is in sinus rhythm. Which treatment is now indicated?
opts: Nitrate infusion

A nitrate infusion is not part of the Takotsubo plan and does not treat a thrombus. The supportive options are beta blockers, anticoagulation if a left ventricular thrombus is present, and diuretics if heart failure is present. Tell: her new finding is a clot, and clot means anticoagulation.
Surgical myectomy

Surgical myectomy is not part of Takotsubo care; treatment is empiric and supportive. Her thrombus in the akinetic apex is treated with anticoagulation. Tell: the new finding is a ventricular clot, and the supportive plan answers it with anticoagulation.
Anticoagulation

Correct. Treatment of Takotsubo cardiomyopathy is empiric and supportive and depends on the presentation, and a thrombus in her akinetic left ventricular apex is the finding that calls for anticoagulation. Beta blockers are helpful, and diuretics are added only if heart failure is present; most patients completely recover.
Pacemaker insertion

A pacemaker is not indicated: she is in sinus rhythm, and nothing suggests a conduction problem. The new finding is a left ventricular thrombus, and Takotsubo care adds anticoagulation when a thrombus is present. Tell: match the treatment to the finding, thrombus to anticoagulant.

set2.q: A 58-year-old woman with idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy has taken a beta blocker, an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor, spironolactone and a diuretic for many months. She still has breathlessness on moderate exertion, and a repeat echocardiogram shows an ejection fraction of 25%. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Implantable cardioverter defibrillator

Correct. She has had many months of maximum medical therapy (beta blocker, angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor, spironolactone and a diuretic), and her ejection fraction is still 25%. An implantable cardioverter-defibrillator is indicated when the ejection fraction is below 35% after maximum medical therapy.
Endomyocardial biopsy to find a cause

Biopsy does not answer her problem, a persistently low ejection fraction on full therapy, and her disease is already labeled idiopathic. The next step for an ejection fraction below 35% after maximum medical therapy is an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator. Tell: 25% after months of treatment meets the device threshold.
Surgical myectomy of the septum

Septal myectomy has no role here: her ventricle is dilated with an ejection fraction of 25%, not obstructed. The device indicated for an ejection fraction below 35% after maximum medical therapy is an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator. Tell: dilated disease is managed with drugs, devices, an assist device or transplant, not septal surgery.
Stopping the beta blocker

Beta-adrenergic blockers are on the core drug list for dilated cardiomyopathy, and stopping hers would remove part of her maximum medical therapy. With an ejection fraction still below 35% on that therapy, she needs an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator. Tell: when maximal drugs fail, add a device rather than subtract a drug.

set2.q: A 71-year-old woman with restrictive cardiomyopathy and marked biatrial enlargement has had palpitations for a week, and the electrocardiogram now shows atrial fibrillation. Which treatment reduces her risk of embolism?
opts: Surgical myectomy

Surgical myectomy is not part of restrictive cardiomyopathy management and does nothing for embolism. With atrial fibrillation and marked biatrial enlargement, she needs anticoagulants to prevent embolism from atrial thrombi. Tell: the question asks about embolism, and only an anticoagulant prevents clots.
A positive inotrope

A positive inotrope is not on the restrictive cardiomyopathy list and does not prevent clots. The listed drugs are diuretics with caution, beta blockers or verapamil and diltiazem, and anticoagulants for atrial thrombi. Tell: embolism prevention means anticoagulation.
Anticoagulation

Correct. In this woman with restrictive cardiomyopathy, marked biatrial enlargement and new atrial fibrillation, anticoagulants may be needed to prevent embolism from atrial thrombi. Beta blockers or verapamil and diltiazem may help filling time, but only anticoagulation addresses the embolic risk.
Aggressive diuresis

Diuretics treat pulmonary and systemic congestion but must be used with caution, because noncompliant ventricles depend on preload to maintain cardiac output, and they do not prevent emboli. Anticoagulants prevent embolism from atrial thrombi. Tell: diuretics for congestion, anticoagulants for clots.

set2.q: A 26-year-old man with suspected viral myocarditis has an elevated troponin and normal coronary arteries. His cardiologist wants to see how much of the heart muscle is inflamed without an invasive procedure. Which test shows the extent of inflammation?
opts: Gadolinium-enhanced cardiac magnetic resonance imaging

Correct. For this man with suspected viral myocarditis, a raised troponin and normal coronary arteries, gadolinium-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging is the noninvasive test that shows the inflammation: gadolinium improves its visibility and shows its extent. Endomyocardial biopsy, the gold standard, is invasive.
Ambulatory rhythm monitoring for forty-eight hours

Rhythm monitoring records the heart's electrical activity over time and cannot image heart muscle; in myocarditis the electrocardiogram may show sinus tachycardia or arrhythmias but not the extent of inflammation. Gadolinium-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging does. Tell: inflammation is seen on enhanced imaging, not on a rhythm strip.
Exercise echocardiography with treadmill testing

Exercise testing is not part of the myocarditis work-up, and an echo is not the test that shows how much muscle is inflamed. Gadolinium-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging improves visibility of inflammation and shows its extent. Tell: the clue is extent of inflammation, which is what gadolinium adds.
Right heart catheterization with pressure tracings

Catheterization is invasive, which the cardiologist wants to avoid, and in myocarditis angiography is used to rule out coronary ischemia, already done here with normal coronaries. Gadolinium-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging shows the extent of inflammation noninvasively. Tell: noninvasive plus extent of inflammation means gadolinium imaging.

set2.q: A 70-year-old woman was admitted with chest pain after a near drowning. Her electrocardiogram showed ST elevation with T-wave inversion, and echocardiography showed hypokinesis of the midsegment and apex of the left ventricle. Which catheterization finding is expected if this is stress cardiomyopathy?
opts: A proximal coronary occlusion

A proximal occlusion would make this acute coronary syndrome, which is what Takotsubo mimics. Stress cardiomyopathy is confirmed by catheterization, which most often shows normal coronary arteries. Tell: her stressor, ST changes and mid and apical hypokinesis point to Takotsubo, whose coronaries are clean.
A ruptured coronary plaque

A ruptured coronary plaque would explain acute coronary syndrome, not stress cardiomyopathy, whose catheterization most often shows normal coronary arteries. Tell: Takotsubo looks like acute coronary syndrome on the electrocardiogram, troponin and echo, and only the coronary arteries tell them apart.
Triple-vessel narrowing

Triple-vessel narrowing would point to coronary disease as the cause of her wall-motion abnormality. In Takotsubo, catheterization most often shows normal coronary arteries. Tell: in this syndrome the coronaries are typically normal, while the echo shows hypokinesis or akinesis of the midsegment and apex.
Normal coronary arteries

Correct. A 70-year-old woman with chest pain after a near drowning, ST elevation with T wave inversion, and hypokinesis of the midsegment and apex of the left ventricle fits stress cardiomyopathy. The diagnosis is confirmed with cardiac catheterization, which most often shows normal coronary arteries.

set2.q: A 48-year-old woman with obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is admitted after surgery with low blood pressure, and a resident proposes a drug to strengthen her heart's contraction. Which drug class should be avoided in her?
opts: Beta blockers such as metoprolol

Beta blockers such as metoprolol are the initial medication for outflow tract obstruction, not a class to avoid. They are negative chronotropes and inotropes that enhance diastolic filling. Tell: the class to avoid is the one that increases contractility, which is what the resident proposed.
Antiarrhythmics such as amiodarone

Amiodarone is used, not avoided: it reduces the incidence and risk of sudden cardiac death with or without outflow obstruction and converts atrial fibrillation and flutter. Positive inotropes are the class to avoid. Tell: the proposal in the stem is a drug to strengthen contraction, and that is the danger.
Calcium channel blockers like verapamil

Verapamil and diltiazem, nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers, are used for outflow tract obstruction as negative chronotropes and inotropes. They are not the class to avoid. Tell: the helpful drugs reduce contractility; the drugs to avoid increase it.
Positive inotropes such as digoxin

Correct. In her obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, a drug to strengthen contraction is exactly what to avoid: positive inotropes such as digoxin, epinephrine and norepinephrine increase contractility, which increases the risk of myocardial ischemia and may induce arrhythmias. Beta blockers do the reverse, decreasing contractility.

set2.q: A 19-year-old woman with a week of fever and myalgia now has severe breathlessness. She is cold and clammy with a blood pressure of 78/50, heart rate 128, raised jugular venous pressure and crackles throughout both lungs. Myocarditis is suspected. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Exercise testing to grade severity

Exercise testing does not belong in the care of a patient with a blood pressure of 78/50 and crackles throughout both lungs. Myocarditis treatment is directed toward the clinical scenario, and hers calls for aggressive hemodynamic stabilization. Tell: an unstable patient is stabilized before any grading.
Aggressive hemodynamic stabilization

Correct. She is hypotensive at 78/50, tachycardic, cold and clammy with raised jugular venous pressure and crackles, a patient in shock. Supportive care is the mainstay of myocarditis treatment, directed toward the clinical scenario, and this scenario requires aggressive hemodynamic stabilization first.
Outpatient follow-up in one week

Outpatient follow-up is unsafe for a patient with a blood pressure of 78/50, a heart rate of 128 and pulmonary crackles. Treatment is directed toward the clinical scenario and may require aggressive hemodynamic stabilization, which comes first. Tell: hypotension and cold, clammy skin rule out sending her home.
Elective biopsy before any support

Endomyocardial biopsy is the gold standard, but it is used once other causes of heart failure are excluded and is not done before support in a patient this unstable. Aggressive hemodynamic stabilization comes first. Tell: diagnosis can follow; her blood pressure of 78/50 cannot wait.

set2.q: A 32-year-old man with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and outflow tract obstruction has breathlessness and chest tightness on exertion. His blood pressure is 124/78 and heart rate is 76. He takes no cardiac medication yet. Which is the initial medication for his outflow obstruction?
opts: A high-intensity loop diuretic

Diuretics reduce preload, and drugs that reduce preload may aggravate outflow tract obstruction; if needed, they are used with caution to avoid dehydration. The initial medication for obstruction is a beta blocker. Tell: obstruction worsens with less filling, so a strong diuretic is the wrong start.
A beta blocker such as metoprolol

Correct. For his outflow tract obstruction with exertional breathlessness and chest tightness, a beta blocker such as metoprolol is the initial medication. As a negative chronotrope and inotrope it reduces heart rate and enhances diastolic filling by reducing ventricular stiffness and decreasing contractility; verapamil or diltiazem is the alternative.
A nitrate such as nitroglycerin

Nitrates reduce preload and afterload, which may increase symptoms by aggravating outflow tract obstruction, so they are avoided if possible. The initial medication is a beta blocker such as metoprolol. Tell: his exertional symptoms come from obstruction, and nitrates make it worse.
A positive inotrope such as digoxin

Digoxin is a positive inotrope, avoided because increased contractility raises the risk of myocardial ischemia and may induce arrhythmias. A beta blocker such as metoprolol, which decreases contractility, is the initial drug. Tell: in obstruction the aim is less squeeze, not more.

set2.q: A 76-year-old man with restrictive cardiomyopathy from cardiac sarcoidosis has two episodes of syncope. His heart rate is 34, and the electrocardiogram shows complete heart block. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Surgical myectomy

Surgical myectomy is not part of restrictive cardiomyopathy management and does nothing for a heart rate of 34 with complete heart block. Conduction system disease from nodal fibrosis is treated with a permanent pacemaker. Tell: syncope with complete heart block needs pacing.
Alcohol septal ablation

Alcohol septal ablation is not part of restrictive cardiomyopathy management and does not treat a slow rhythm. His complete heart block with syncope comes from fibrosis of the sinoatrial and atrioventricular nodes and needs a permanent pacemaker. Tell: block plus syncope means a pacemaker, whatever the underlying disease.
Endomyocardial biopsy

A biopsy does not treat symptomatic complete heart block, and his cause, cardiac sarcoidosis, is already known. Treating the underlying disorder matters, but his conduction disease needs a permanent pacemaker now. Tell: two syncopal episodes at a rate of 34 call for treatment, not more diagnosis.
Permanent pacemaker

Correct. His syncope, heart rate of 34 and complete heart block fit conduction system disease: in restrictive cardiomyopathy, fibrosis of the sinoatrial and atrioventricular nodes can lead to heart block. A permanent pacemaker is the treatment for this conduction disease.

set2.q: A 60-year-old man has just been diagnosed with symptomatic idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy and an ejection fraction of 25%. He asks what his long-term outlook is. Which statement about his prognosis is most accurate?
opts: Nearly all recover fully in weeks

Complete recovery in most patients describes Takotsubo (stress) cardiomyopathy, not symptomatic dilated cardiomyopathy. His outlook is poor overall, with 50% mortality at 5 years. Tell: recovery belongs to the transient stress syndrome; dilated disease is progressive.
Worst outlook of any heart muscle disease

The poorest prognosis among all heart muscle diseases belongs to restrictive cardiomyopathy. Dilated cardiomyopathy is poor too, with 50% mortality at 5 years once symptoms emerge. Tell: poorest of all is restrictive; half dead at 5 years is dilated.
A normal life span without therapy

Symptomatic dilated cardiomyopathy is progressive, with 50% mortality at 5 years, and prognosis depends on response to medical therapy. Tell: progressive disease plus sudden cardiac death from arrhythmia rules out a normal life span, and advanced cases may need an assist device or transplantation.
About half die within five years

Correct. For a man with newly symptomatic idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy, prognosis depends on response to medical therapy but is poor overall, with 50% mortality at 5 years once symptoms emerge. Deaths come largely from the progressive nature of the disease and sudden cardiac death due to arrhythmia.

set2.q: A 66-year-old man with stable cardiomyopathy on full medical therapy says he tires after walking a block and feels anxious about exercising. He has no symptoms at rest. Which referral is most appropriate to improve his exercise tolerance?
opts: A competitive sports clearance clinic

Competitive sport is not a goal for a man who tires after walking a block, and clearance would not build his tolerance. The referral that improves exercise tolerance and quality of life is a cardiac rehabilitation program. Tell: his anxiety also fits rehabilitation, which includes psychological support.
A cardiac rehabilitation program

Correct. His problems are limited exercise tolerance and anxiety about exercising, and cardiac rehabilitation programs aim to improve exercise tolerance and quality of life. Rehabilitative care also provides education on medication adherence, nutrition and symptom monitoring, and psychological support for coping with chronic illness.
Hospice referral for end-stage care

Hospice referral is for end-stage cardiomyopathy. He is stable on full therapy with no symptoms at rest, so the referral that fits is cardiac rehabilitation, which aims to improve exercise tolerance and quality of life. Tell: stable disease with a function goal points to rehabilitation, not end-of-life care.
Genetic screening of his children

Screening his children does nothing for his own exercise tolerance, which is the stated goal. Cardiac rehabilitation programs aim to improve exercise tolerance and quality of life, with education and psychological support. Tell: the question asks about him and his exercise, which rehabilitation addresses.

set2.q: A 71-year-old woman with restrictive cardiomyopathy has fatigue and exercise intolerance along with leg edema, hepatomegaly and ascites, but her lungs are relatively clear. Which pattern of heart failure is expected to dominate in this condition?
opts: Isolated left-sided failure

Isolated left-sided failure does not fit her relatively clear lungs. Restrictive cardiomyopathy raises filling pressures in both ventricles, and right heart failure may dominate, giving hepatomegaly, bilateral pedal edema and ascites. Tell: congestion in the abdomen and legs with clear lungs points right.
High-output heart failure

High-output failure does not fit, because her exercise intolerance comes from poor cardiac output. Right heart failure may dominate in restrictive cardiomyopathy, matching her edema, hepatomegaly and ascites. Tell: restrictive disease lowers output, and the dominant side is the right.
Pure systolic failure

Pure systolic failure is not the pattern described; the restrictive problem is raised filling pressure in both ventricles, and right heart failure may dominate over left. Tell: her leg edema, hepatomegaly and ascites are right-sided findings, and the question asks which side dominates.
Right-sided heart failure

Correct. Her leg edema, hepatomegaly and ascites with relatively clear lungs are the right-sided pattern. In restrictive cardiomyopathy, filling pressures are elevated in both ventricles, but right heart failure may dominate over left, with an elevated jugular venous pressure, bilateral pedal edema and ascites.

set2.q: A 17-year-old boy with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy asks his clinician what the most serious risk of his disease is. He has occasional palpitations and plays recreational basketball. Which complication is the leading cause of death in this condition?
opts: Embolic stroke

Embolic stroke is not the leading cause of death in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Sudden cardiac death is, while heart failure symptoms progress gradually in others. Tell: for a young athlete with this disease, the danger to name is sudden death.
Aortic dissection

Aortic dissection is not part of the hypertrophic cardiomyopathy course. The leading cause of mortality is sudden cardiac death, with heart failure symptoms progressing more slowly. Tell: the leading killer in this disease is sudden and cardiac, not vascular.
Sudden cardiac death

Correct. For this teenager with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and palpitations, the most serious risk is sudden cardiac death, the leading cause of mortality in the disease. Patients are classically advised to keep to mild to moderate, noncompetitive activity, stay hydrated and avoid excess alcohol.
Progressive heart failure

Heart failure symptoms do gradually progress in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, and transplantation is an option if the disease stops responding to therapy, but sudden cardiac death is the leading cause of mortality. Tell: progressive failure is the slow course; sudden death is the leading cause.

set2.q: A 67-year-old woman with suspected restrictive cardiomyopathy has right-sided heart failure and big atria on echocardiogram. Her cardiologist wants to measure pressures inside both ventricles to characterize the filling problem. Which invasive test evaluates ventricular pressure tracings?
opts: Exercise echocardiography

Exercise echocardiography is noninvasive and does not record pressures inside the ventricles; the echo in restrictive cardiomyopathy shows big atria and abnormal diastolic function but is not definitive. Ventricular pressure tracings come from cardiac catheterization. Tell: the stem asks for an invasive pressure test.
Cardiac catheterization

Correct. To measure pressures inside both ventricles, the cardiologist needs cardiac catheterization, which is useful in restrictive cardiomyopathy to evaluate ventricular pressure tracings. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging adds information when the cause is unclear, and biopsy is reserved for specific situations.
Endomyocardial biopsy

Endomyocardial biopsy samples tissue to confirm or exclude a diagnosis that would change management, usually after negative imaging and genetic testing; it does not record pressures. Ventricular pressure tracings come from cardiac catheterization. Tell: tissue says what the disease is; a catheter says what the pressures are.
Transesophageal echocardiogram

A transesophageal echocardiogram is still an echocardiogram, and echo alone is not definitive in restrictive cardiomyopathy. Direct ventricular pressure tracings require cardiac catheterization. Tell: pressure tracings mean a catheter inside the heart.

set2.q: A 60-year-old man with dilated cardiomyopathy has orthopnea (breathlessness lying flat), crackles at both lung bases and diminished breath sounds at the right base. A chest radiograph is ordered. Which finding on the film would indicate pulmonary edema?
opts: Short horizontal lines meeting the pleura

Correct. His orthopnea and basal crackles suggest pulmonary edema, and on the chest radiograph Kerley B lines, horizontal lines 1 to 2 cm long meeting the pleura at right angles, indicate it. The diminished breath sounds at his right base fit the pleural effusion and cardiomegaly that dilated cardiomyopathy also shows.
A small heart with clear lung fields

A small heart with clear lungs is the opposite of the expected film: dilated cardiomyopathy shows cardiomegaly, pleural effusions and pulmonary edema. Tell: with crackles and diminished breath sounds at the right base, expect a large heart and fluid on the film.
A normal film that excludes congestion

A normal film would not fit his crackles and diminished breath sounds; the radiograph in dilated cardiomyopathy shows cardiomegaly, pleural effusions and pulmonary edema, sometimes as Kerley B lines. Tell: the question asks for a sign of edema, and a normal film offers none.
Isolated thickening of the pericardium

Pericardial thickening is not a chest radiograph sign of pulmonary edema and is not among the dilated cardiomyopathy film findings. Pulmonary edema shows as Kerley B lines, short horizontal lines meeting the pleura at right angles. Tell: edema is in the lungs, so its sign is in the lung fields.

set2.q: A 45-year-old man presents with new-onset heart failure a week after a flulike illness. He smokes and has hyperlipidemia, so the team wants to exclude coronary disease before labeling this myocarditis. Which test rules out coronary ischemia as the cause of his new heart failure?
opts: Sedimentation rate

The erythrocyte sedimentation rate may be elevated in myocarditis, but it says nothing about the coronary arteries. Cardiac angiography rules out coronary ischemia as the cause of new heart failure. Tell: to exclude coronary disease, look at the coronaries.
Chest radiograph

The chest X-ray is nonspecific and may show cardiomegaly, but it cannot show the coronary arteries. Cardiac angiography rules out coronary ischemia as the cause of new-onset heart failure. Tell: a nonspecific test cannot exclude a specific cause.
Cardiac angiography

Correct. Cardiac angiography is used in the myocarditis work-up to rule out coronary ischemia as a cause of new-onset heart failure. That matters for this man, whose smoking and hyperlipidemia give him coronary risk, before his heart failure after a flulike illness is labeled myocarditis.
Endomyocardial biopsy

Endomyocardial biopsy is the gold standard used once other causes of heart failure have been excluded, so it comes after the coronary question is answered. Cardiac angiography rules out coronary ischemia. Tell: biopsy confirms myocarditis; angiography excludes the coronary alternative.

set2.q: A 64-year-old man has restrictive cardiomyopathy confirmed on imaging, but cardiac magnetic resonance imaging and genetic testing have not identified a cause. His team is considering endomyocardial biopsy. When is biopsy performed in this condition?
opts: Only after cardiac transplantation is done

Biopsy belongs to the diagnostic work-up, done when imaging and genetic testing are negative or when tissue could change management, not only after transplantation. Tell: his team is still searching for a cause, which is exactly when biopsy is used.
Never, since it cannot change management

Biopsy is performed precisely when a tissue sample could confirm or exclude a diagnosis that would change clinical management, or when imaging and genetic testing are negative. Tell: never contradicts the stated indications, and his situation matches one of them.
When imaging and genetic tests are negative

Correct. In restrictive cardiomyopathy, endomyocardial biopsy is performed when all imaging studies and genetic testing are negative, or when a tissue sample is likely to confirm or exclude a diagnosis that would change management. His negative magnetic resonance imaging and genetic testing meet the first condition.
As the first test in every suspected case

Biopsy is not the first test. The echocardiogram, then cardiac magnetic resonance imaging when no cause is found, come first, and biopsy follows negative imaging and genetic testing. Tell: biopsy sits at the end of the sequence, after the noninvasive tests.

set2.q: A 47-year-old man has new dilated cardiomyopathy with an ejection fraction of 30%. He reports fatigue, heat intolerance and weight loss, and the conjunctivae look pale. Which initial laboratory tests are most useful for finding a contributing cause?
opts: Blood cultures and a throat swab

Cultures are not part of the dilated cardiomyopathy laboratory panel, and nothing in his story points to infection. The panel is a complete blood count for anemia, a metabolic panel for electrolytes and renal function, liver function and thyroid function. Tell: his heat intolerance and pallor match thyroid tests and a blood count.
Urine osmolality and cortisol

Neither test is part of the listed work-up. His clues match two tests that are: thyroid function for heat intolerance and weight loss, and a complete blood count for pale conjunctivae. Tell: hyperthyroidism is on the dilated cardiomyopathy differential, so thyroid function is checked.
Thyroid function and a blood count

Correct. His heat intolerance and weight loss raise hyperthyroidism, which is on the dilated cardiomyopathy differential, and his pale conjunctivae raise anemia. The initial work-up includes thyroid function and a complete blood count to evaluate for anemia, along with a metabolic panel and liver function.
Serum lipase and amylase levels

Lipase and amylase are not part of the dilated cardiomyopathy work-up. The listed tests are a complete blood count for anemia, a metabolic panel, liver function and thyroid function. Tell: heat intolerance, weight loss and pallor match thyroid tests and a blood count.
