set2.q: A 26-year-old woman with obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is leaving for a summer hiking trip in a hot climate. She takes a beta blocker and asks how to lower her risk of symptoms while away. Which counseling point is most appropriate?
opts: Take extra diuretic on hot days

Extra diuretic in the heat runs straight against the advice to maintain hydration and avoid dehydration. Tell: in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, anything that dries the patient out works against the self-care she has been taught, which also includes avoiding excess alcohol.
Use alcohol to relax at the campsite

Patients with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy are taught to avoid excess alcohol consumption, alongside maintaining hydration. Using alcohol to relax at camp contradicts that advice. Tell: in this disease alcohol appears only on the avoid list.
Stay well hydrated; avoid dehydration

Correct. Patients with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy are advised to maintain hydration and avoid dehydration, which matters on a hot-weather hiking trip. The same education covers avoiding excess alcohol and keeping to mild to moderate, noncompetitive recreational activity.
Restrict fluids to soften the murmur

Fluid restriction contradicts the advice to maintain hydration and avoid dehydration, and softening the murmur is not a goal of self-care. Tell: a hot-climate trip makes hydration the key counseling point, along with avoiding excess alcohol.

set2.q: A 73-year-old woman has just been diagnosed with restrictive cardiomyopathy from amyloidosis. She has right-sided heart failure and asks how her condition compares with other kinds of heart muscle disease. Which statement about her prognosis is most accurate?
opts: Poorest of all heart muscle diseases

Correct. Restrictive cardiomyopathy has the poorest prognosis among all types of heart muscle disease. Management treats the underlying disorder, such as her amyloidosis, uses diuretics with caution and anticoagulants or a pacemaker as needed, and ends with cardiac transplantation.
Complete recovery within weeks

Complete recovery within weeks is not the restrictive course; this disease carries the poorest prognosis among all heart muscle diseases, with transplantation as the final option. Tell: the restrictive outlook is the worst, not the best.
A normal life span with diuretics

Diuretics are used for pulmonary and systemic congestion, with caution because noncompliant ventricles depend on preload, but they do not change the outlook. Restrictive cardiomyopathy has the poorest prognosis of all heart muscle diseases. Tell: symptom relief is not the same as a normal life span.
Better than other cardiomyopathies

The opposite is true: restrictive cardiomyopathy has the poorest prognosis among all types of heart muscle disease. Tell: remember restrictive as the worst outlook, with cardiac transplantation as the last option.

Echocardiogram shows abnormal diastolic filling, normal-sized ventricles and big atria, but the team cannot tell restrictive cardiomyopathy from constrictive pericarditis. Which test is used to differentiate them?
opts: Ambulatory rhythm monitoring

Rhythm monitoring records rhythm, which in restrictive disease often shows atrial fibrillation or conduction disorders, but it does not show the pericardium. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging differentiates the two by showing pericardial thickening in pericarditis. Tell: telling these apart needs an image of the pericardium.
Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging

Correct. Echocardiography alone is not definitive because restrictive cardiomyopathy and constrictive pericarditis look alike, as in this man with big atria and abnormal diastolic filling. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging is used to differentiate them, showing pericardial thickening in pericarditis.
Repeat transthoracic echocardiogram

Echocardiography alone is not definitive for this distinction, so repeating it adds little. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging is used to differentiate them, showing pericardial thickening in pericarditis. Tell: a test that could not settle the question once will not settle it on repeat.
Exercise stress echocardiogram

An exercise echo is still an echocardiogram, and echo alone is not definitive for separating restrictive cardiomyopathy from constrictive pericarditis. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging is used, showing pericardial thickening in pericarditis. Tell: the answer is a different modality, not a different echo.

set2.q: A 15-year-old boy is seen for a sports physical. He has no symptoms, but his father was recently diagnosed with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, which is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern. Which strategy for this adolescent is most appropriate?
opts: Genetic screening for the condition

Correct. Age-specific care for adolescents includes genetic screening for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, which fits a 15-year-old whose father has the autosomal dominant disease. Activity restriction is added for high-risk individuals, with medication for symptoms and an implantable defibrillator in select cases.
Waiting until adulthood to evaluate

Screening is listed as an adolescent strategy, so waiting until adulthood skips the step meant for his age. Genetic screening for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is the fit. Tell: the age-specific list places genetic screening in adolescence, and he is 15.
A routine chest radiograph each year

A yearly chest radiograph is not among the adolescent strategies. The listed approach is genetic screening for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, with activity restriction for high-risk individuals. Tell: with an affected father and a dominant pattern, the screening tool is genetic.
An endomyocardial biopsy at this visit

Biopsy is not part of the adolescent strategy, and he has no symptoms. Genetic screening for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is the listed approach for adolescents, with activity restriction if high risk. Tell: an asymptomatic relative is screened, not biopsied.

opts: Genetic testing to guide therapy

Genetic testing is available in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy but does not influence treatment, so it offers her no new therapy. Cardiac transplantation is the option for disease unresponsive to conventional therapy. Tell: a test that does not influence treatment cannot be the treatment option.
Cardiac transplantation

Correct. In hypertrophic cardiomyopathy heart failure symptoms gradually progress, as hers have over several years, and cardiac transplantation is the option when the disease is unresponsive to conventional therapy. Sudden cardiac death remains the leading cause of mortality.
Digoxin to boost contraction

Digoxin is a positive inotrope, avoided in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy because increased contractility raises the risk of myocardial ischemia and may induce arrhythmias. Transplantation is the option for refractory disease. Tell: boosting contraction is on the avoid list in this disease.
Daily nitrates for comfort

Nitrates reduce preload or afterload and are avoided if possible because they may increase symptoms by aggravating outflow tract obstruction. Transplantation is the option when conventional therapy fails. Tell: a drug on the avoid list cannot be the answer for refractory disease.

set2.q: A 38-year-old woman with obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy still has disabling breathlessness despite a beta blocker and later verapamil. Echocardiogram shows systolic anterior motion (the anterior mitral leaflet pulled into the outflow tract) with mitral regurgitation. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Permanent pacemaker alone

A pacemaker alone does not remove the thickened septum that obstructs her outflow tract. Surgical myectomy excises part of the septal myocardium, and alcohol septal ablation is the catheter alternative. Tell: refractory obstruction needs the septum reduced.
Long-term nitrate therapy

Nitrates do not reduce the septum and are not among the next-step options; after drug failure, the choices for outflow obstruction are surgical myectomy or alcohol septal ablation. Tell: her problem is a mechanical obstruction with mitral regurgitation, which myectomy relieves and may resolve.
Escalating loop diuretics

More diuretic does not relieve septal obstruction. Surgical myectomy excises part of the septal myocardium in outflow obstruction, and the mitral regurgitation may resolve with it. Tell: drugs have failed, so the next step is reducing the septum.
Surgical septal myectomy

Correct. Her obstruction is refractory to a beta blocker and verapamil, so surgical myectomy, which excises part of the septal myocardium causing outflow obstruction, is the next step. Replacement of the mitral valve may or may not be needed, because the mitral regurgitation may resolve with myectomy.

set2.q: A 52-year-old woman with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy has new palpitations. Her pulse is irregularly irregular and the electrocardiogram shows atrial fibrillation. Echocardiogram shows left atrial enlargement. Which treatment prevents embolic stroke in her?
opts: Anticoagulation

Correct. In hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, atrial fibrillation, as in this woman with an irregularly irregular pulse and left atrial enlargement, is treated with anticoagulation to prevent embolic stroke. Antiarrhythmics such as amiodarone convert and suppress it, and radiofrequency ablation is another option.
Digoxin for rate control

Digoxin is a positive inotrope avoided in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy because increased contractility raises ischemia risk and may induce arrhythmias. It does not prevent stroke; anticoagulation does. Tell: stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation means anticoagulation.
Nitrate therapy

Nitrates reduce preload or afterload and are avoided if possible because they may aggravate outflow tract obstruction; they do nothing to prevent emboli. Anticoagulation prevents embolic stroke. Tell: the question asks about stroke, which only an anticoagulant addresses.
Diuretic therapy

Diuretics may be necessary but are used with caution to avoid dehydration, and they do not prevent thromboembolism. Anticoagulation is the stroke-prevention step in atrial fibrillation. Tell: amiodarone controls the rhythm; anticoagulation protects against stroke.

set2.q: A 30-year-old man is diagnosed with dilated cardiomyopathy. His father had a cardiomyopathy and his older brother died suddenly at 35. No alcohol, drug or chemotherapy exposure is found. Which is the most appropriate referral for him and his family?
opts: Family screening only after age 60

Waiting until 60 makes no sense when his brother died suddenly at 35. Genetic counseling for patients with a family history is part of dilated cardiomyopathy care now. Tell: the family history is already present, so counseling starts at diagnosis.
Genetic counseling for the family

Correct. His father's cardiomyopathy and his brother's sudden death at 35 are a family history, with no alcohol, drug or chemotherapy cause found. Patient education in dilated cardiomyopathy includes genetic counseling for patients with a family history, alongside removing any offending source and sodium restriction.
Reassurance that it is not inherited

Reassurance ignores his father's cardiomyopathy and his brother's sudden death at 35. Genetic counseling is recommended for patients with a family history. Tell: with no alcohol, drug or chemotherapy cause, the family history is the lead to follow.
Heart biopsies for his relatives

Heart biopsies are not a family strategy. The step for a patient with a family history of dilated cardiomyopathy is genetic counseling, part of patient education alongside medication follow-up. Tell: relatives are counseled, not biopsied.

set2.q: A 79-year-old man with cardiomyopathy has become lightheaded on standing since his medications were increased at his last visit. He is frail and has lost weight. Which parts of his drug therapy call for particular caution at his age?
opts: Diuretics and vasodilators

Correct. Age-specific care for elderly patients calls for cautious use of diuretics and vasodilators, with therapy tailored to comorbidities and frailty and a focus on symptom control and quality of life. His lightheadedness on standing after a dose increase, with frailty and weight loss, is the situation that caution targets.
Sodium restriction advice

Sodium restriction is a lifestyle modification listed for adults, not a drug, so it is not the drug therapy the question asks about. The medications singled out for caution in the elderly are diuretics and vasodilators. Tell: his symptoms began when medications were increased.
Home-based rehabilitation

Home-based rehabilitation is an option for elderly or mobility-limited patients and is not a drug. Caution in the elderly applies to diuretics and vasodilators. Tell: the question asks about drug therapy, and the elderly list names two drug classes.
Implanted device checks

Device therapy is part of adult cardiomyopathy care, but device checks are not drug therapy and do not explain lightheadedness after a medication increase. The elderly list calls for cautious use of diuretics and vasodilators. Tell: link his symptom to the drug change.

set2.q: A 46-year-old man who has drunk heavily for 20 years has six months of worsening breathlessness on exertion and orthopnea (breathlessness lying flat). The apical impulse is displaced laterally and a third heart sound (an early diastolic sound just after the second heart sound) is heard. Echocardiogram shows dilated, thin-walled ventricles with an ejection fraction of 25%, and coronary angiography shows no significant narrowing. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Stress cardiomyopathy

Stress cardiomyopathy does not fit six months of steadily worsening symptoms with globally dilated, thin-walled ventricles. Dilation and impaired contraction without severe occlusive coronary disease define dilated cardiomyopathy. Tell: a slow course and dilated chambers point to dilated disease, not a sudden reaction to a stressor.
Dilated cardiomyopathy

Correct. Dilated, thin-walled ventricles with an ejection fraction of 25% and no significant coronary narrowing fit dilated cardiomyopathy: myocardial dysfunction with dilation and impaired contraction in the absence of severe occlusive coronary artery disease. The result is systolic dysfunction, here in a man with 20 years of heavy drinking.
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy

Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy means thick walls, but his ventricles are dilated and thin-walled; dilated cardiomyopathy increases cardiac mass with little or no wall hypertrophy. Tell: thin, dilated walls with an ejection fraction of 25% point to dilated, not hypertrophic, disease.
Restrictive cardiomyopathy

Restrictive cardiomyopathy is not the picture of dilated ventricles with impaired contraction; that combination, with systolic dysfunction and an ejection fraction of 25%, defines dilated cardiomyopathy. Tell: his displaced apical impulse and third heart sound fit a big, weak ventricle.
